title: Theory Stretch: Modes, Transposition & Advanced Intervals
welcome_lead: Push beyond major and minor — explore modes, transposition and the subtler details of intervals.

final_note: You can read, transpose and analyse music at an advanced GCSE level.

concepts.def: A scale type — e.g. Dorian, Mixolydian — used in folk and jazz.
Rewriting music at a different pitch.
Notes spelled differently but sounding the same (F♯ = G♭).
4th, 5th and octave — neither major nor minor.
An interval larger than an octave.
Augmented 4th — three whole tones, very tense.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Modes are scales formed by starting a major scale on a different note. Dorian (D to D on white notes) sounds minor but brighter; used in folk and 'Scarborough Fair'.

Mixolydian (G to G white notes) sounds major but with a flat 7; used in rock and Celtic music.

To transpose up a tone: every note moves up two semitones, and the key signature shifts accordingly. C major up a tone = D major (2 sharps).

Transposing instruments (clarinet in B♭, horn in F) sound a different pitch from what is written — composers must transpose to keep parts playable.

4ths, 5ths and octaves are perfect. 2nds, 3rds, 6ths and 7ths can be major or minor.

An augmented interval is a semitone wider than perfect/major; a diminished interval is a semitone narrower. The famous tritone (augmented 4th) was once nicknamed the 'devil in music'.
